ComprehensionText:
"A principal fruit of friendship," Francis Bacon wrote in his timeless meditation on the subject, "is the ease and discharge of the fulness and swellings of the heart, which passions of all kinds do cause and induce." For Thoreau, friendship was one of life's great rewards. But in today's cultural landscape of muddled relationships scattered across various platforms for connecting, amidst constant debates about whether our Facebook "friendships" are making us more or less happy, it pays to consider what friendship actually is. That's precisely what CUNY philosophy professor Massimo Pigliucci explores in Answers for Aristotle: How Science and Philosophy Can Lead Us to A More Meaningful Life (public library), which also gave us this provocative read on the science of what we call "intuition."

Philosophers and cognitive scientists agree that friendship is an essential ingredient of human happiness. But beyond the dry academic definitions — like, say, "voluntary interdependence between two persons over time, which is intended to facilitate socio-emotional goals of the participants, and may involve varying types and degrees of companionship, intimacy, affection and mutual assistance" — lies a body of compelling research that sheds light on how, precisely, friendship augments happiness.

The way friendship enhances well-being, it turns out, has nothing to do with quantity and everything to do with quality — researchers confirm that it isn't the number of friends (or, in the case of Facebook, "friends")

AnswerA: Bacon and Thoreau's theories are no longer available to read
AnswerB: The arrival of social media on the scene
AnswerC: There is more interest in the sciences
AnswerD: Friendships are not possible in the real world anymore, due to over- competition

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
1 If you've spent any time in grocery checkout lines, you've probably seen magazines with pictures of celebrities behaving badly toward each other. You might believe that scientists would be above that sort of thing, but you'd be wrong. About 150 years ago, two scientists started a nasty feud that lasted for decades— and brought to light some of the most spectacular creatures that ever walked the earth.

2 Edward Cope and Othniel Marsh were paleontologists—scientists who study extinct life-forms, including dinosaurs. They met in 1864, when their careers were starting. Paleontology was a young science in the United States, and only a few dinosaurs had been discovered in North America. Othniel Marsh Edward Cope

3 Cope and Marsh were friendly at first, but their relationship quickly soured. In 1868, Cope and a team of hired men were digging up dinosaurs in New Jersey. Marsh journeyed there and stayed with Cope for a few weeks. Things seemed to go well, but after Marsh left, Cope learned that his guest and the team foreman had made a deal. In exchange for money, the foreman would send new fossils to Marsh instead of Cope. Marsh had fired the first shot in what scientists would come to call the "Bone Wars."

4 The war heated up fast. In 1869, Cope wrote an article describing a newly found extinct sea reptile he named Elasmosaurus. Cope included a drawing of the creature's skeleton. Another scientist soon pointed out that Cope had mistakenly stuck the beast's skull on its tail. Cope was humiliated, and Marsh crowed about the blunder to anyone who would listen. Shortly after, each man began publishing a string of scientific articles viciously attacking the other's ideas.

Interim Assessment Unit 1

5 Cope and Marsh's thirst to outdo each other spilled into their fieldwork. Throughout the 1870s and 1880s, they led and sent teams into lawless regions of the western United States to hunt for dinosaur bones. The teams were told to slow and disrupt each other's work through bribery, stealing, and rock-throwing. The teams even used dynamite to blow up cliffs and bury fossils to keep discoveries from falling into each other's hands. To this day, scientists wonder what fantastic discoveries lay beneath tons of rubble.

6 In addition to sabotage, Cope and Marsh forced their teams to dig up and transport bones quickly. Such speed damaged many specimens, but each man wanted the credit of making the first discoveries of new species. Because they published their findings as quickly as possible, they made many mistakes. Marsh, for example, accidentally stuck the head of one dinosaur (Camarasaurus) on to the neck of another dinosaur (Apatosaurus) and thought he had discovered a new dinosaur—Brontosaurus. Unlike Cope's mistake with Elasmosaurus, paleontologists didn't discover and undo Marsh's Brontosaurus blunder for nearly 100 years.

7 Until the mid-1880s, only scientists knew about Cope and Marsh's fight. But when Cope ratted out Marsh to the New York Herald, their battle spilled out into the world at large. Cope and Marsh assaulted each other through letters published in the newspaper. For a time, they were as famous as any celebrities of today. And even when the public eventually stopped caring, the feud didn't cease. The two men of science took swipes at each other until Cope's death in 1897. Even in death, Cope kept up the attack. He donated his skull to science and asked that his brain size be compared with Marsh's. (Scientists of that time believed that a person with a large brain was smarter than a person with a small one.) For whatever reason, Marsh did not accept Cope's challenge.

8 The Bone Wars have a mixed legacy.

On the one hand, American paleontology got a bad reputation from Cope and Marsh's cutthroat behavior. And the mistakes they made in their rush for glory slowed the progress of paleontology for many years. But the Bone Wars also produced a mountain of raw material.

Cope and Marsh discovered more than

130 dinosaur species. Their teams dug up so many bones that scientists are still learning new things about them. And many of their most famous discoveries, including Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Diplodocus, and Triceratops, fire the imaginations of children (and more than a few adults) worldwide. Perhaps paleontology would have been worse off had the two men actually gotten along.
QuestionText: The article says that paleontology was a young science in the United States in the mid-1800s. How knowledgeable about the field were paleontologists of the time?
AnswerA: They were more informed than those in other nations.
AnswerB: They were the greatest experts of the field at the time.
AnswerC: They were not very knowledgeable about their field.
AnswerD: They were just as knowledgeable as any other scientists.

1 You're a fish in the ocean.

3 O.K., so you're not a fish. And this sci-fi fishland doesn't exist. But it could—not long from now.

4 Allow me to introduce SoFi—like "Sophie," but short for "Soft Robotic Fish," revealed in Science Robotics, by scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab.

9 SoFi started as a nine-inch silicon tail that wiggled with the assistance of a hydraulic pump.

Page 8 Session 2

10 "I was amazed at how well it was working, how well I was able to get this tail to beat back and forth or swim left and right, like a shark or some other fish," said Robert Katzschmann, a graduate student at MIT who led the team. 13 "We wanted to build a fish," said Mr. Katzschmann. "And the fish can't be as big as a submarine—unless we wanted to build a whale."

14 A couple years later SoFi had a finned body and head equipped with a camera, twoway hydrophone, battery, environmental sensors, operating system and communication system that allowed a diver to issue commands using a souped-up Super Nintendo controller.

3 O.K., so you're not a fish. And this sci-fi fishland doesn't exist. But it could—not long from now.

4 Allow me to introduce SoFi—like "Sophie," but short for "Soft Robotic Fish," revealed in Science Robotics, by scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab.

5 They explained how their finned robot was created, and how her first ocean swim on a coral reef outside of Fiji went. 6 This foot-and-a-half long robot mimics a real fish. She can swim in the ocean at speeds up to half-its-body-length a second and at depths up to 60 feet below the surface. SoFi has a battery that will last 45 minutes before she shuts down.

9 SoFi started as a nine-inch silicon tail that wiggled with the assistance of a hydraulic pump.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Out of Tune
My cello and I arrived at Riverside Hall forty minutes early, which turned out to be thirty-nine minutes too many. There is only so long you can sit in a cramped backstage room, listening to other people warm up, before your stomach starts turning cartwheels.
I was playing 'The Swan', a slow, gentle piece I had practised every day for two months. Ms Varga, my teacher, had made me play it so many times that I could hear it in my sleep. At our last lesson, she had given me one piece of advice. 'If something goes wrong, don't stop,' she said. 'An audience follows the music, not the mistakes. If you keep going, most of them will never know.'
I nodded, but privately I thought nothing would go wrong. I knew every note.
Backstage, the only free chair was beside an old electric heater that clanked and hissed in the corner. I propped my cello against the wall next to it and spent the next half-hour reading the program over and over, as if my name might vanish from it.
At last the stage manager called, 'Sam Taylor, you're on.'
The lights were brighter than I had expected, and the hall was full. Somewhere in the third row sat my grandfather, who had driven two hours to be there. I placed my bow on the strings and began.
The first few lines went beautifully. The notes floated out over the audience exactly the way Ms Varga had taught me. Then, halfway through, I reached for a high note on the A string, and something was badly wrong. The note came out flat, sour and wobbly, like a singer who has forgotten the tune. I tried the next note. That was flat too. My string had slipped out of tune.
For one terrible second my bow froze. I could feel hundreds of eyes on me. My hand wanted to stop, put the cello down and run.
Then I heard Ms Varga's voice in my head: don't stop.
So I didn't. I kept the bow moving and listened harder than I had ever listened in my life. If the string was low, I would have to place my fingers a little higher to find the right sound. It felt strange and awkward, like writing with the wrong hand, but slowly the notes began to sound right again. I reached the final long note, let it fade into silence and lifted my bow.
The applause was loud and warm. My grandfather was clapping above his head.
Afterwards, Ms Varga found me in the corridor. She tapped the cello's tuning peg and raised an eyebrow. 'You left it next to the heater, didn't you?' Then she smiled. 'Nicely rescued.'
My grandfather told me it was the best thing he had heard all year. He hadn't noticed a thing.

AnswerA: Ms Varga, the teacher
AnswerB: Sam, the young cellist
AnswerC: Sam's proud grandfather
AnswerD: the stage manager

ComprehensionText:
When Words Swap Places
Have you ever meant to say "a crushing blow" and heard yourself say "a blushing crow" instead? If so, you have made a spoonerism: a slip of the tongue in which the first sounds of two words swap places. The result is often nonsense, sometimes oddly poetic, and nearly always funny.
Spoonerisms are named after William Archibald Spooner, a kindly, white-haired teacher at Oxford University in England more than a hundred years ago. Spooner was said to mix up his words so often that his students began collecting his mistakes. He supposedly scolded one lazy student for having "hissed all my mystery lectures", and is said to have told another that he had "tasted a whole worm" when he meant "wasted a whole term". Before long, any such slip was simply called a "spoonerism".
There is just one problem with these famous stories: most of them are probably not true. Spooner admitted to only a few slips, and historians suspect that his students invented many of the best ones, polishing them for laughs and passing them on. Spooner reportedly found his fame rather tiresome. Even so, the name stuck.
Whether Spooner said them or not, slips like these are real, and scientists who study language find them fascinating. When you speak, your brain does not choose one word at a time. It plans several words ahead, lining up the sounds before you say them. Occasionally, a sound from a word that is coming up jumps the queue and lands in the wrong place. That is why spoonerisms almost always swap sounds in matching positions, such as the beginnings of two words, and why the mixed-up result usually still sounds as if it could be English. Even when we make mistakes, our brains follow the rules. Researchers have even caused spoonerisms on purpose in experiments, by flashing pairs of words on a screen and asking volunteers to read them aloud as quickly as possible.
In other words, a spoonerism is not a sign of a careless mind. It is a tiny window into how busy and organised our brains are while we talk.
Spoonerisms have also become a favourite toy for writers and comedians, who make them up on purpose. Here is a limerick built around one:
An usher, with manners so neat,
Met a lady who'd come off the street.
With a bow and a smile
He led her down the aisle,
And said, "Let me sew you to your sheet!"
So if you ever make a spoonerism yourself, there is no need to feel embarrassed. You are in good company. Just smile, correct yourself and carry on. After all, a brain that can swap sounds so neatly is running like a well-boiled icicle.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Mrs Lang's Fairy Books
In 1889, a book with a bright blue cover appeared in London bookshops. The Blue Fairy Book gathered old tales such as "Cinderella", "Rumpelstiltskin" and "Beauty and the Beast", and it sold so well that a Red Fairy Book followed the next year. By 1910 there were twelve volumes, each named after a different colour. Every one carried the same name: Andrew Lang. Yet the person who did most of the writing was barely mentioned.
Leonora Blanche Alleyne was born in 1851 and in 1875 married Andrew Lang, a Scottish scholar and journalist. Andrew was fascinated by folklore and believed fairy tales deserved serious study, not merely a place in the nursery. He was also extraordinarily busy, turning out poems, essays, histories and newspaper columns at a startling pace.
Leonora had a gift for languages. As the fairy book project grew, she took on the task of turning stories from French, German, Spanish, Italian and other languages into lively English. She did not simply translate word for word. She reshaped each tale for young readers, trimming slow passages and softening details that seemed too gruesome for a Victorian nursery. In time she oversaw a small team of translators, most of them women, and polished their work into one consistent voice.
Andrew's role was mainly to choose the stories' themes, write the prefaces and lend his famous name, which helped the books sell. He never pretended to have done everything. In the preface to The Lilac Fairy Book, the final volume, he stated plainly that the books had been almost wholly the work of Mrs Lang. Few readers noticed. The covers did not change, and for generations, children and librarians spoke of "Andrew Lang's fairy books".
Leonora also published books under her own name, including The Red Book of Heroes and The Book of Princes and Princesses. These attracted far less attention than the coloured series.
Why did she stay in the background? Part of the answer lies in the customs of the time. Victorian publishers believed a well-known male author would attract buyers, and many women writers accepted that their work would be credited to someone else. How Leonora herself felt about this is not well recorded.
Today, historians of children's literature are giving her more credit. The coloured fairy books helped decide which tales English-speaking children grew up with, and Leonora's choices about what to keep, what to soften and what to cut still echo through countless picture books and films. She was, in a sense, the invisible gatekeeper of the fairy-tale kingdom.

AnswerA: They believed men were better translators.
AnswerB: They wanted to hide that the tales were old.
AnswerC: They wanted to keep Leonora's name private.
AnswerD: They believed it would attract more buyers.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
A Voice in the Shoebox
Four per cent. Tess watched the number on her phone as if staring at it might stop it shrinking. The storm had torn through the valley overnight, and since dawn the farmhouse had been silent: no fridge hum, no lights, no internet. Pop said the power lines were down somewhere near the highway, but nobody knew how long repairs would take.
At three per cent, she switched the phone off and slumped at the kitchen table.
Pop disappeared into the shed and came back with a dusty shoebox. Inside was a tangle of copper wire, a cardboard tube, a tiny glass part no bigger than a grain of rice, and an old earpiece on a cord.
"More junk?" Tess asked.
"A radio," said Pop. "Or it will be, once we build it."
For the next hour they worked side by side. Tess wound the thin wire around the cardboard tube, a hundred careful turns, while Pop scraped the ends bare with his pocketknife. He showed her how to join the tiny glass part, which he called a diode, to the coil and the earpiece. Then they carried a long reel of wire outside, and Pop climbed a ladder to tie one end high up on the windmill. A second wire ran from the shoebox to the metal garden tap.
"Where does the battery go?" Tess asked, searching the box.
"There isn't one," Pop said. "The radio station's tower sends out radio waves day and night, and each wave carries a little energy. By the time they reach us, there's only a whisper of it left, so we need a big net to catch enough. The longer and higher the aerial, the more we catch."
Tess pressed the earpiece to her ear. Nothing. Pop slid a metal clip slowly along the coil. Still nothing, then a crackle, and then, so faint she had to hold her breath, a man's voice.
"...crews are working to restore power to the valley, and supply is expected back by early evening..."
"It's working!" Tess whispered, as if speaking aloud might frighten the voice away. The man was talking from a studio more than a hundred kilometres away, and his words were reaching her through a cardboard tube and some wire, with nothing to power them but the waves themselves.
Just after six, the fridge shuddered back to life and every light in the house came on at once. Tess's phone, charging on the bench, buzzed with a stream of messages.
She didn't look at it. The news had finished, and the announcer was playing an old country song. Tess sat on the back step with the earpiece pressed to her ear, watching the windmill turn slowly against the pink sky, and listened until the very last note.

AnswerA: soft
AnswerB: loud

AnswerD: slow
